1 Assignment Overview

We provide, as an entirely optional supplement to the required course materials, an assignment on training language models to follow instructions and aligning language models to pairwise preference judgments.

What you will implement

1. Zero-shot prompting baselines for a variety of evaluation datasets.

2. Supervised fine-tuning, given demonstration data with instruction-response pairs.

3. Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) for learning from pairwise preference data.

What you will run

1. Measure Llama 3.1 8B zero-shot prompting performance.

2. Instruction fine-tune Llama 3.1 8B.

3. Fine-tune Llama 3.1 8B on pairwise preference data.

What you can use

As in the main assignment, we expect you to build the core components from scratch. You may use tools like vLLM to generate text from language models, and Hugging Face Transformers to load Llama models and tokenizers. You may not use training utilities such as the Trainer class.

2 Motivation: Training Generalist LLMs

In contrast to the required assignment, which focuses on reasoning models, we will now turn to building generalist dialogue systems that can handle a wide range of natural language processing tasks. We will walk through the process of setting up evaluations, collecting fine-tuning and preference data, and using this data to make a language model that is much more capable of following user instructions and refusing malicious ones.

As representative downstream tasks, we will measure factual knowledge (MMLU; [D. Hendrycks et al., 2021]), reasoning (GSM8K; [K. Cobbe et al., 2021]), chatbot quality (AlpacaEval; [X. Li et al., 2023]), and safety (SimpleSafetyTests; [B. Vidgen et al., 2024]).

2.1 Models and shared volumes

The base model that we will be training and evaluating is meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B. Some parts of the assignment will involve automatic judging, for which we will use meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct.

These models are large, so to avoid re-downloading the models, we have provided the model weights in a shared volume cs336-a5-supplement on Modal. We also provide a modal_utils_safety.py file, which mounts the shared volume to /mnt/cs336-a5-supplement when running commands. The

modal_utils_safety.py file also specifies the paths to the model weights, along with the UltraChat-200K dataset. Please do not write to the shared volume.

The assignment will also involve saving trained checkpoints and loading them later. To save checkpoints or results and access them later, you should mount cs336-a5-supplement-results-{SUNET_ID} to the path /mnt/cs336-a5-supplement-results and write to that path, as specified in modal_utils_safety.py. Once again, please do not write to the shared volume.

3 Zero-Shot Evaluation

As in the main assignment, we will start by establishing zero-shot baselines for each of the tasks, in order to understand how each of our post-training steps affect model behavior.

We’ll be working with the Llama 3.1 8B base model, so we’ll measure its performance. Since our goal is to build a general-purpose assistant that can handle a variety of tasks, we’ll use the same system prompt on all tasks. This prompt is provided in cs336_alignment/prompts_safety/zero_shot_system_prompt.prompt.

In the prompt blocks below, the ↪ symbol marks a visual line continuation in the PDF. It is not part of the prompt string, and it does not denote a newline.

CODE / INTERFACE 
# Instruction
Below is a list of conversations between a human and an AI assistant (you).
Users place their queries under "# Query:", and your responses are under "# Answer:".
CS336 · Assignment 05 · Supplement2 / 18
SOURCE PAGE 03 / 18
CODE / INTERFACE 
You are a helpful, respectful, and honest assistant.
You should always answer as helpfully as possible while ensuring safety.
Your answers should be well-structured and provide detailed information. They should
↪ also have an engaging tone.
Your responses must not contain any fake, harmful, unethical, racist, sexist, toxic,
↪ dangerous, or illegal content, even if it may be helpful.
Your response must be socially responsible, and thus you can reject to answer some
↪ controversial topics.

# Query:
```{instruction}```

# Answer:
```

With this system prompt, the expectation is that the model generates the answer, closes the Markdown code block with three backticks, and then starts the next conversation turn with # Query:. Thus, when we see the string # Query:, we can stop response generation.

3.1 Zero-Shot MMLU Baseline

Prompting setup. To evaluate zero-shot performance on MMLU, we’ll load the examples and prompt the language model to answer the multiple choice question. Since the language model simply outputs freeform text, it isn’t always trivial to evaluate its outputs.

In this case, naively prompting the language model with our system prompt and an MMLU example means that it’ll sometimes output the letter corresponding to the correct answer, the text of the correct answer, or even a paraphrased version of the correct answer. These variations can make it complex to parse the answer from the model’s generations.

As a result, properly evaluating these models often requires specifying a particular answer format in the prompt. In the case of MMLU, we’ll use the following task prompt from cs336_alignment/

prompts_safety/mmlu_zero_shot.prompt:

CODE / INTERFACE 
Answer the following multiple choice question about {subject}. Respond with a single
↪ sentence of the form "The correct answer is _", filling the blank with the letter
↪ corresponding to the correct answer (i.e., A, B, C or D).

Question: {question}
A. {options[0]}
B. {options[1]}
C. {options[2]}
D. {options[3]}
Answer:

In the prompt above, {subject} refers to the subject split of the MMLU example (e.g., high school

geography), {question} is the question text (e.g., Which of the following is a centrifugal force in a

country?), and {options} is the list of multiple-choice options (e.g., ["Religious differences", "A

national holiday", "An attack by another country", "A charismatic national leader"]).

For zero-shot evaluation, first format this task prompt with the MMLU example, then insert the formatted task prompt into the {instruction} placeholder in cs336_alignment/prompts_safety/

zero_shot_system_prompt.prompt. Generate from that full prompt.

To evaluate the model’s outputs on each instruction, prompt an annotator model to assess whether it prefers our model’s generated output or the generated output of a reference model. 4 Instruction Fine-Tuning

From inspecting the outputs of the zero-shot baseline model, you may have noticed that it can often be difficult to get language models to reliably follow instructions via prompting alone. In this part of the assignment, we’ll explicitly fine-tune Llama 3.1 8B to follow instructions. Training a language model on data with paired prompt-response demonstrations is often called instruction fine-tuning or supervised fine-tuning (SFT).

4.1 Looking at Instruction Tuning Data

To instruction fine-tune our language models, we’ll use a mix of data from the UltraChat-200K dataset1 and the SafetyTunedLlamas dataset2. This data has been processed into a single-turn format, where each example contains a single prompt and a single response.

We’ve placed the data on the Modal shared volumes at the following paths:

1. /mnt/cs336-a5-supplement/data/safety_augmented_ultrachat_200k_single_turn/train.jsonl.gz

2. /mnt/cs336-a5-supplement/data/safety_augmented_ultrachat_200k_single_turn/test.jsonl.gz

Each line is a JSON object with keys prompt and response.

4.2.1 Data Loader

Our instruction fine-tuning dataset is a collection of prompt-response pairs. To fine-tune our language models on this data, we need to convert these prompt-response pairs to strings. We’ll use the following template from Alpaca, provided in cs336_alignment/prompts_safety/alpaca_sft.prompt (note that this prompt differs from the zero_shot_system_prompt.prompt we used in the previous section). As before, ↪ marks a visual line continuation in the PDF and is not part of the prompt:

CODE / INTERFACE 
Below is an instruction that describes a task. Write a response that appropriately
↪ completes the request.

### Instruction:
{instruction}

### Response:
{response}

We can treat these strings as documents for language modeling and train our models on this data. As with other types of data, we concatenate all of these documents into a single sequence of tokens, adding a delimiter between them, such as the Llama 3.1 8B end-of-text token.

A data loader turns this sequence of tokens into a stream of batches, where each batch consists of 𝐵 sequences of length 𝑚, paired with the corresponding next tokens, also of length 𝑚.

In practice, examples are often packed into constant-length sequences, which minimizes padding tokens and thus maximizes GPU throughput. To break our sequence of token IDs into chunks of length 𝑚, we’ll take consecutive, non-overlapping chunks of size 𝑚, dropping the final chunk if it has fewer than 𝑚 tokens. For example, given token IDs [0, 1, 2, ..., 9, 10] and desired sequence length 4, potential batch inputs would be [[0, 1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6, 7]]. Iterating over the data loader should return each of these inputs exactly once, which constitutes an epoch over the data.

4.2.2 Training Script

Now that we’ve implemented a data loader for our instruction fine-tuning data, we’ll write a training script to fine-tune a pre-trained Llama 3.1 8B base model.

Loading the model for fine-tuning. Use Hugging Face transformers. We’ll load the model in

bfloat16 and use FlashAttention-2 to save memory:

CODE / INTERFACE 
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name_or_path)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_name_or_path,
    torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    attn_implementation="flash_attention_2",
)

Computing language modeling loss. After loading the model, run a forward pass on a batch of input IDs and get logits via the .logits attribute. Then compute the loss between the model’s predicted logits and labels:

CODE / INTERFACE 
input_ids = train_batch["input_ids"].to(device)
labels = train_batch["labels"].to(device)

logits = model(input_ids).logits
loss = F.cross_entropy(..., ...)

Saving the trained model. Save the model to a directory with save_pretrained. We recommend saving the tokenizer as well, even if you did not modify it, so the model and tokenizer are self-contained and loadable from a single directory:

CODE / INTERFACE 
model.save_pretrained(save_directory=output_dir)
tokenizer.save_pretrained(save_directory=output_dir)

Gradient accumulation. Despite loading the model in bfloat16 and using FlashAttention-2, even a large GPU may not support the effective batch size you want. With the setup above, you should be able to train on sequences of 512 tokens with a small per-device batch size. However, we prefer to use a larger effective batch size, such as 32 sequences per gradient step.

Gradient accumulation accomplishes this by accumulating gradients over several microbatches before taking an optimizer step. Intuitively, if we had a larger GPU, we should get the same result from computing the gradient on a batch of 32 examples all at once versus splitting them into 16 batches of 2 examples each and averaging at the end.

Normally, we run a forward pass, call loss.backward(), call optimizer.step(), and then zero the gradients:

CS336 · Assignment 05 · Supplement10 / 18
SOURCE PAGE 11 / 18
CODE / INTERFACE 
for inputs, labels in data_loader:
    logits = model(inputs)
    loss = loss_fn(logits, labels)

loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
    optimizer.zero_grad()

To implement gradient accumulation, call optimizer.step() and optimizer.zero_grad() every 𝑘 steps, where 𝑘 is the number of gradient accumulation steps. Divide the loss by gradient_accumulation_steps before calling loss.backward() so the gradients are averaged:

CODE / INTERFACE 
gradient_accumulation_steps = 4
for idx, (inputs, labels) in enumerate(data_loader):
    logits = model(inputs)
    loss = loss_fn(logits, labels) / gradient_accumulation_steps
    loss.backward()

if (idx + 1) % gradient_accumulation_steps == 0:
        optimizer.step()
        optimizer.zero_grad()

As a result, the effective batch size is multiplied by 𝑘.

ASSIGNMENT TASKp. 11
Problem (sft):  Instruction tuning (3 B200 hrs) (6 points)

Fine-tune Llama 3.1 8B base on the instruction tuning data. We recommend training for a single epoch using context length 512 and total batch size 32 sequences per gradient step. Save both model and tokenizer after training, since we will evaluate them and use them later for DPO.

We used learning rate 2e-5, cosine decay, linear warmup over 3% of total training steps, weight decay 0.1, and gradient clipping at 1.0. It may be useful to experiment with learning rate to build intuition.

Deliverable: A description of your training setup, the final validation loss, a learning curve, and the serialized model/tokenizer.

6 “Reinforcement Learning” From “Human Feedback”

During SFT, we train our model to imitate responses from a given set of high-quality examples. Still, that is often not enough to mitigate undesired behavior learned during pretraining. While SFT relies on an external set of good examples, for aligning language models it is often helpful to elicit responses from the model itself that we are trying to improve, and reward or penalize those responses based on some assessment of their quality and appropriateness.

A method that gained popularity recently for its use in the OpenAI models was Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback, or RLHF [L. Ouyang et al., 2022]. In RLHF, we start with a set of prompts to be given to our model after SFT. Then, we elicit sets of responses from the model to each prompt. The

CS336 · Assignment 05 · Supplement14 / 18
SOURCE PAGE 15 / 18

“Reinforcement Learning” part of RLHF comes from the fact that we do not get a per-token loss, as we have in SFT, since in that setting we are given a reference response. Instead, we train the model to optimize for a scalar reward signal that measures how appropriate a complete response is for a given prompt. The “HF” indicates that, at least in the original method, this reward signal was obtained from fitting a model on data from human annotators, who manually ranked the given sets of responses.

The original RLHF method is fairly intricate. After SFT, we first generate 𝐾 responses for each prompt and have humans rank them, which is expensive to do at scale. Then, RLHF proposes to explicitly fit a reward model 𝑟𝜃(𝑥,𝑦), which assigns a scalar reward for a response 𝑦 given prompt 𝑥. Here, 𝑟𝜃 starts as the SFT model with the final output layer removed and an extra layer that outputs a scalar value. Then, sample prompts 𝑥 and pairs of responses 𝑦𝑤, 𝑦𝑙 from the human preferences dataset, where 𝑦𝑤 was ranked better than 𝑦𝑙, and optimize:

Intuitively, we want the reward model to output scalar rewards that agree with rankings from human annotators. This loss is lower when there is higher agreement between the reward model and the human data.

After fitting a reward model, RLHF proceeds by optimizing the LM using RL, where the LM is a policy 𝜋𝜃 that receives a prompt and chooses a token to generate at each step until it finishes its response. At that point it receives a reward from 𝑟𝜃. The original paper used Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) for training the LM using the reward model. The paper describing RLHF on GPT-3 models also found it important to add a KL-divergence penalty to prevent the model from deviating too much from the SFT model and to include an auxiliary pretraining language-modeling objective to avoid degenerating downstream performance.

RLHF has many moving parts, and has reportedly been difficult to reproduce beyond the success that OpenAI had applying it. More recently, another method for aligning models with preference data, Direct Preference Optimization (DPO; [R. Rafailov et al., 2023]), has become widely popular for both its simplicity and effectiveness, producing models that often perform on par with or better than models trained with RLHF. In the last part of this assignment, you will implement DPO and experiment with using it to align models using preference labels.

6.1 The DPO Objective

In RLHF, we first explicitly fit a reward model 𝑟𝜃 using collected preference data, and then optimize the LM to generate completions that receive high reward. DPO starts from the observation that instead of first finding an optimal reward model 𝑟 and then finding an optimal policy 𝜋𝑟 for that reward model, we can derive a reparameterization of the optimal reward model represented in terms of the optimal policy itself:

Here, 𝜋ref is the reference policy: the original LM after SFT that we do not want to deviate too much from. The parameter 𝛽 controls the strength of the penalty for deviating from 𝜋ref. The policy 𝜋𝑟 is the optimal policy for reward model 𝑟. The second term only depends on an instruction-dependent normalization constant 𝑍(𝑥), not on completion 𝑦.

The original per-instance reward-model loss in Equation 1 only depends on differences between rewards assigned to different completions. When we take the difference, the partition function cancels out, giving the simpler per-instance DPO loss:

CS336 · Assignment 05 · Supplement15 / 18
SOURCE PAGE 16 / 18

To compute this loss, we do not need to sample completions during the alignment process as in RLHF. All we need is to compute conditional log-probabilities. Thus, there is no explicit reinforcement learning happening. The preference data need not necessarily come from human annotators either: several works have had success applying these methods on preferences generated by other language models, often prompted to judge pairs of alternative responses to the same query.

6.2 Looking at Preference Data

Before using preference data to align our LMs, it is useful, as always, to look at the data yourself and make sense of it. We will first use both prompts and completions from the HH dataset (“Helpful and Harmless”) collected by Anthropic. We will leverage the training set of four collections in the dataset, obtained using many different human-written prompts: harmless-base, helpful-online, helpful-base, and helpful-rejection-sampled.

The current data directory contains:

CODE / INTERFACE 
data/hh/harmless-base.jsonl.gz
data/hh/helpful-base.jsonl.gz
data/hh/helpful-online.jsonl.gz
data/hh/helpful-rejection-sampled.jsonl.gz

These are only the training splits. Each gzipped file is in JSON-lines format, where each line contains a valid JSON object. Each object has a chosen conversation between a human and the assistant, preferred by the human annotator, and a rejected conversation, both starting from the same prompt.

6.3 Implementing the DPO Loss

We’ll now start our implementation of DPO, which we’ll use to align our LM using the preference datasets we looked at. You will implement the per-instance DPO loss in Equation 3, given a pair of LMs, the LM we’re optimizing and the reference model, and a pair of responses to the same prompt 𝑥: the preferred response 𝑦𝑤 and rejected response 𝑦𝑙. Since we’re dealing with large models, the two models might not be on the same device. Return the loss on the same device as the LM being optimized.

When computing a difference of conditional log-probabilities under the same model, such as log 𝜋𝜃(𝑦𝑤| 𝑥) −log 𝜋𝜃(𝑦𝑙| 𝑥), the prompt probability cancels. Therefore, this is equivalent to the difference of unconditional log-probabilities for the concatenated strings concat(𝑥, 𝑦𝑤) and concat(𝑥, 𝑦𝑙).

6.4 DPO Training

You will now implement a training loop using DPO on the HH data. Unlike during SFT, we now have to run two examples through the LMs, 𝜋ref and 𝜋𝜃, to compute the loss, which takes significant GPU memory. Thus, we will not try to batch our implementation, and will use gradient accumulation, as done in SFT, to allow for larger effective batch sizes. Similarly, we won’t use AdamW unless we use other efficiency tricks such as quantization, so we will stick to RMSprop, as also done in the original DPO work. We suggest the following implementation path, which sacrifices maximal performance for simplicity:

1. Use 2 GPUs, one for the reference model and one for the trained model.

2. Load two copies of your instruction fine-tuned model, one on each device.

3. Separate out a small number of examples, such as 200, as a validation set.

4. Train your model with DPO loss and gradient accumulation, tracking your loss at each step.

5. Start with effective batch size 64, 𝛽= 0.1, and learning rate 1e-6.

Besides these tricks, keep track of the “classification accuracy” of the implicit reward model on the validation set. This simply amounts to comparing the log-probability of chosen and rejected completions, considering an example correctly classified when the chosen completion has higher log-probability.
